newsitem.title: GERMANY: Pressure on Waigel to wrap up German tax reform.
newsitem.headline: Pressure on Waigel to wrap up German tax reform.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel came under renewed pressure on Tuesday from critics within Chancellor Helmut Kohl's ruling alliance to complete tax reform proposals this week after a messy and damaging debate.

Key elements of the tax reform remained open after leaders from Kohl's three-party coalition met on Monday. A tax policy working group, chaired by Waigel, will meet for the last time on Wednesday ahead of final coalition talks a day later.

A debate over raising value-added tax has stolen the limelight from the main element of Waigel's reform -- income tax cuts intended to be the centrepiece of Kohl's bid for a record fifth election win next year.
Peter Hintze, general secretary of Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU), told German television a decision on VAT may have to await progress on reforming the social security system.
The issue of the ratio between direct and indirect taxes is broader than the question of tax reform, Hintze said. "Whether we get that done on Thursday, we will have to see," he said.
Waigel has come under attack from a group of young CDU politicians, dubbed the "wild bunch" by German media, who say he has failed to deliver the government's tax-cutting message.
Led by Christian Wulff, a leading party official in Lower Saxony, the clique has called for Waigel to resign if he fails to rule out a VAT hike when he announces his final reform plans on Thursday.
Wulff and his up-and-coming party friends won the guarded support of CDU deputy parliamentary leader Heiner Geissler, who, however, stopped short of calling for Waigel to step down.
"Why can't we criticise? There are good reasons to," Geissler told German Radio on Tuesday. "We live in a democracy, and rows and debates belong to democracy."

Kohl on Monday repeated his defence of long-time friend Waigel. The Finance Minister called the attacks improper and underhand, and said they were really aimed at Kohl and heir apparent, CDU parliamentary leader Wolfgang Schaeuble.
With Kohl in Prague on Tuesday to sign a joint declaration of Czech-German reconciliation, little progress was expected on the tax front.
That leaves two income tax proposals still in play.
Waigel favours cutting the top rate of income tax in 1999 to 39 percent from 53 percent. Taxes would rise on a sliding scale from an entry point of 19.5 percent, down from 26 percent now.
An alternative concept still being pushed by the Free Democrats (FDP), junior partners in Kohl's 14-year government, calls for three tax brackets of 15, 25 and 35 percent.
Corporation tax would fall to 35 percent from 47 percent.

Waigel wants to abolish a range of tax breaks and raise VAT by one percentage point to 16 percent to partly cover the tax cuts -- leaving taxpayers 25 billion marks ($15.41 billion) better off at the end of the day. But some CDU leaders want a two-point VAT rise to ease the load on Germany's stretched social security system.
With the government in turmoil over tax reform, the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) have been gloating from the sidelines.

"The Bonn coalition has begun the new year as it ended the old: in chaos and infighting," SPD party manager Franz Muentefering said in a statement. "Nobody should forget that the leader of this gang is called Kohl."
Ordinary Germans seemed none too impressed by the Bonn in-fighting.

"I find this whole discussion unworthy, and it makes a mockery of the taxpayer," one woman told German radio in a vox-pop interview. Another said: "They should put a result on the table and stop all this palaver."
